sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Anthropic lifts Nasdaq futures and tech stocks ahead of its record-breaking IPO
sources.text: This is CNBC's Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox. Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today's edition of Morning Squawk. A historic IPO for markets and an exclusive for CNBC. Andrew Ross Sorkin will speak to Anthropic co-Founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei at 10 a.m. ET, as the biggest public listing in history starts trading on the Nasdaq. Anthropic has priced its IPO above the expected range, at $83 per share . With around 980 million shares sold, it has raised $81.3 billion, surpassing SpaceX's record IPO back in June. Anthropic's fully diluted market cap sits at around $1.5 trillion. The stock is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq today under the ticker symbol "ANT." CNBC's Leslie Picker will report from the Nasdaq throughout the trading day. Nasdaq futures are higher in anticipation, as traders gear up for this historic moment. Shares in chipmakers and companies that are invested in Anthropic are also higher premarket. Shares in Nvidia are gaining in premarket trading, alongside other tech heavyweights Amazon , Alphabet and Broadcom . Palo Alto shares are jumping over 9% in premarket trading, after the group raised its annual revenue forecast. The move is also pulling cybersecurity shares higher too. An unprecedented trilateral summit has taken place between U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. In Shenzhen, China, each leader spoke about the importance of their "special responsibility" to ensure global peace. Here are some key quotes: CNBC's Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning. It's the most anticipated video game in a generation. After 13 long years, gamers can finally play "Grand Theft Auto VI" as its global rollout gets underway. It's not just players rejoicing; investors are also applauding the blockbuster release. Shares in the studio behind the game, Take-Two Interactive , traded higher on the revenue boost. Kash Patel skips House hearing after Mar-a-Lago gala with $50,000 access After a string of outages disrupted airlines , banks and even the National Security Agency , U.S. House members gathered Wednesday to question the nation's top security officials. But FBI Director Kash Patel was nowhere to be seen. The night before, Patel and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had been advertised as "honored guests" at the Big Blue Bash , a lavish charitable fundraiser at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, where attendees were offered access to a "private roundtable" and a stay at the venue for $50,000 a person . — CNBC's Ashley Capoot, Leslie Picker, Greg Iacurci, Julia Boorstin, Luke Fountain, and Samantha Subin contributed to this report.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself
sources.text: After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models. Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday. The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models. “The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?” Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth. The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates. Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since . For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures , shifting priorities , and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks. Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring , while operating losses are declining . Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures. Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money. The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.) Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries . Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives. Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there. Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top issue. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit. At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
sources.text: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO. At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for. Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy. However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.” With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting. $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry. Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest. Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day. 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%. The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says. More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater. Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet. All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run. stories.title: Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatens 'tremendous tax'
stories.summary: Trump spoke at the White House after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a historic trilateral summit in China.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatens 'tremendous tax'
sources.text: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." Trump's latest push for more data-center construction in the U.S. came despite Americans repeatedly stating — and showing with their votes — that they dislike the structures. CNBC's All-America Economic Survey found that 64% of registered voters opposed an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% of respondents said they would support one. If Trump follows through on his threat to clamp down on overseas data center construction, he will have to contend with the fact that numerous U.S. tech giants — including Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta and Oracle — have already built them in other countries. International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements. Trump said Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them." "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump said. The remarks came a day after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China for a trilateral summit that appeared to produce few concrete deliverables on an array of pressing global issues. Xi "congratulated me on how well we're doing" in artificial intelligence, Trump said, using his preferred term "super intelligence," which he said the Chinese president also likes better. This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates. — CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed reporting.

sources.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
sources.text: While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.﻿ While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.﻿ President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them. “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.” Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.” Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative. Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks: Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside. We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind. So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

stories.title: Maior IPO da história: Anthropic supera desconfiança com IA e vale mais que a SpaceX, de Ellon Musk
stories.summary: Criadora do Claude captou US$ 107 bilhões, superando os US$ 75 bilhões da SpaceX. Avaliada em US$ 1,5 trilhão, empresa atrai investidores com forte crescimento, mas enfrenta custos bilionários para sustentar a expansão.

sources.name: Convergencia Digital
sources.title: Maior IPO da história: Anthropic supera desconfiança com IA e vale mais que a SpaceX, de Ellon Musk
sources.text: Em um momento que a Inteligência Artificial está sob críticas – até por conta dos ataques hackers originados com o uso da tecnologia – os investidores cravam que a demanda por ferramentas de inteligência artificial continuará crescendo, à medida que empresas de diferentes setores ampliem o uso desses serviços. E o resultado é que a Anthropic, dona do Claude, faz nesta quinta-feira (19) a maior estreia de uma empresa na bolsa de valores da história. A criadora do Claude movimentou US$ 107 bilhões (R$ 629 bilhões) com a venda de ações, superando os US$ 85,7 bilhões (R$ 504,1 bilhões) captados pela SpaceX em junho. A empresa arrecadou US$ 81,3 bilhões (R$ 478,3 bilhões) com a venda de 980 milhões de ações, a um preço médio de US$ 83 (R$ 488) por papel. Além disso, levantou outros US$ 26 bilhões com a venda de ações para grandes investidores, como Google, Nvidia e AMD. Além do valor captado, a estreia chama a atenção pela avaliação de US$ 1,5 trilhão (R$ 8,8 trilhões) atribuída à companhia. Esse cálculo representa o valor de mercado estimado da empresa como um todo, e não apenas os recursos que entrarão em seu caixa com a venda de ações. Segundo dados apresentados à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC, na sigla em inglês), a empresa registrou faturamento de US$ 33,2 bilhões (cerca de R$ 194,55 bilhões) nos primeiros nove meses de 2026, mais de sete vezes o valor de US$ 4,585 bilhões (R$ 26,87 bilhões) registrado em todo o ano de 2025. Esse crescimento também aparece no número de clientes corporativos. No fim de setembro, mais de 11,9 mil empresas haviam gerado, cada uma, pelo menos US$ 100 mil (R$ 586 mil) em receita para a Anthropic nos 12 meses anteriores. Cerca de 250 delas haviam superado US$ 10 milhões (R$ 58,6 milhões) em receita no mesmo período. O aval foi dado, mas especialistas afirmam que um dos principais desafios da Anthropic é o custo de acompanhar o crescimento da inteligência artificial. Desenvolver modelos mais avançados e atender a um número cada vez maior de usuários exige investimentos contínuos em computadores, data centers e infraestrutura.

sources.name: Canaltech
sources.title: Anthropic levanta US$ 81 bi no maior IPO da história e supera SpaceX
sources.text: Por Marcelo Fischer | 19/11/2026 às 17:03 A Anthropic, empresa responsável pela inteligência artificial (IA) Claude, estreou na bolsa de valores dos Estados Unidos nesta quinta-feira (19) após levantar US$ 81,3 bilhões (cerca de R$ 481,5 bilhões) na maior oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO) da história. Os papéis abriram em alta de 34%, levando a companhia a atingir um valor de mercado estimado em US$ 2 trilhões . A empresa iniciou as negociações na Nasdaq, bolsa de tecnologia de Nova York, sob o código ANT. Cada ação foi vendida inicialmente por US$ 83, mas começou a ser negociada a US$ 111,50, segundo a Reuters. Com o resultado, a Anthropic superou o recorde estabelecido pela SpaceX, de Elon Musk, em junho deste ano, e se tornou a primeira das principais desenvolvedoras de modelos avançados de IA a abrir seu capital. A valorização inicial, entretanto, perdeu força ao longo do dia. No início da tarde, as ações eram negociadas abaixo dos US$ 100, enquanto as bolsas americanas registravam perdas em meio às preocupações dos investidores com os altos custos da inteligência artificial. O IPO é o processo pelo qual uma empresa passa a negociar suas ações publicamente pela primeira vez, permitindo que investidores comprem participações em seu negócio. No caso da Anthropic, foram ofertadas 980 milhões de ações a US$ 83 cada , valor superior à faixa inicialmente prevista de US$ 70 a US$ 78. O preço estabelecido na operação avaliou a companhia em aproximadamente US$ 1,5 trilhão, considerando também ações que poderão ser emitidas futuramente. Segundo o comunicado oficial, cerca de 956,4 milhões de ações foram vendidas pela própria Anthropic. As outras 23,6 milhões pertenciam a acionistas que aproveitaram a operação para negociar parte de suas participações. A empresa também autorizou os bancos responsáveis pela oferta a vender até 147 milhões de ações adicionais, o que poderá elevar o valor total do IPO para aproximadamente US$ 93,5 bilhões. Paralelamente, a Anthropic recebeu US$ 26 bilhões em uma colocação privada de ações, com a participação de empresas como Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD e Broadcom, segundo a Reuters. Somando as duas operações, o volume de recursos negociados ultrapassa US$ 107 bilhões. Parte desse dinheiro, porém, corresponde à venda de participações por acionistas existentes e não entra diretamente no caixa da Anthropic. A estreia da Anthropic foi acompanhada de forte volatilidade nas bolsas americanas. Depois de abrir a US$ 111,50 e superar momentaneamente os US$ 115, a ação perdeu parte dos ganhos e chegou à faixa dos US$ 97 no início da tarde. Mesmo após o recuo, os papéis permaneciam cerca de 17% acima do preço definido no IPO. O resultado demonstra o interesse dos investidores pela empresa, mas também evidencia as oscilações que podem ocorrer no primeiro dia de negociação. A movimentação aconteceu em um dia de perdas para os principais índices de Wall Street. Por volta das 12h45, no horário de Nova York, o S&P 500 caía 1,1%, enquanto o Nasdaq recuava 1% e o Dow Jones perdia 1,5%, segundo a Associated Press. Na Europa, as bolsas também fecharam em baixa. De acordo com a CNN Brasil, o índice FTSE 100, de Londres, caiu 0,93%, enquanto o DAX, da Alemanha, recuou 0,92%, e o CAC 40, da França, perdeu 0,81%. A queda dos mercados europeus também foi influenciada por tensões geopolíticas no Oriente Médio e pela guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia. Algumas empresas ligadas à fabricação de semicondutores, entretanto, registraram ganhos. A holandesa ASML avançou 2,2%, enquanto a ASM International subiu 3,1%. Fundada em 2021 pelos irmãos Dario e Daniela Amodei e outros ex-funcionários da OpenAI, a Anthropic cresceu principalmente com a comercialização dos modelos Claude e de ferramentas como o Claude Code, voltado à programação. A empresa registrou uma receita de US$ 16,96 bilhões no terceiro trimestre de 2026 , crescimento de 47% em relação aos três meses anteriores. Ao final de outubro, a receita anualizada, calculada a partir do ritmo recente de vendas, havia chegado a US$ 81 bilhões. Os investimentos necessários para sustentar esse crescimento também aumentaram. Segundo documentos apresentados pela Anthropic, a companhia gastou aproximadamente US$ 9 bilhões com infraestrutura e capacidade computacional apenas no primeiro semestre de 2026. No terceiro trimestre, a empresa registrou prejuízo operacional de US$ 567 milhões. O prejuízo líquido foi de US$ 23,3 bilhões, influenciado por ajustes contábeis relacionados a títulos conversíveis em ações. Esses números ajudam a explicar por que o IPO é acompanhado de perto por investidores e analistas. Há dúvidas sobre a capacidade das empresas de inteligência artificial de transformar os investimentos bilionários em infraestrutura em lucros sustentáveis. A estreia também coloca pressão sobre a OpenAI, principal concorrente da Anthropic e responsável pelo ChatGPT. A expectativa é que a companhia avance com seus próprios planos de abertura de capital em 2027. O IPO ocorre após um período de preocupação com a possibilidade de uma bolha no setor. Em outubro, o Canaltech mostrou que a avaliação pretendida pela Anthropic havia sofrido um corte de US$ 500 bilhões durante as negociações com investidores. Veja também: Afinal, o que é IPO?
